'''''Leonotis leonurus''''', also known as '''wild dagga''' and '''lion's ear''', is a plant species in the mint family [[Lamiaceae]]. It is a broadleaf evergreen [[shrub]], native to [[Flora of South Africa|South Africa]], where it is very common, with a wide altitudinal range from 5 m up to 1980 m.<ref name="sanbi">{{cite web | title=Leonotis leonurus | website=PlantZAfrica | date=2014-07-21 | url=https://pza.sanbi.org/leonotis-leonurus | access-date=2025-07-09}}</ref> It is known to have medicinal and sedating properties. The main psychoactive component of ''Leonotis leonurus'' is hypothesized to be either [[leonurine]] or a mixture of [[labdane]]-type compounds;<ref name="Ho2015">{{cite book |author=Wing Shing Ho |title=Active Phytochemicals from Chinese Herbal Medicines: Anti-Cancer Activities and Mechanisms |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=n3xjCgAAQBAJ&pg=PA39 |date=4 September 2015 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=978-1-4822-1987-6 |pages=39–}}</ref> ''Leonotis leonurus'' has been confirmed to contain leonurine according to peer reviewed journal published phytochemical analysis.<ref name="phytojournal.com">{{cite journal |url=https://www.phytojournal.com/vol3Issue6/Issue_march_2015/3-6-21.1.pdf |title=''Leonotis leonurus'': A herbal medicine review |author=Ofentse Mazimba |journal=Journal of Pharmacognosy and Phytochemistry |date=2015 |volume=3 |issue=6 |pages=74–82 |access-date=17 May 2022}}</ref> Like other plants in the mint family, it also contains [[marrubiin]]. The word "dagga" comes from [[Afrikaans]], and derives in turn from the [[Khoikhoi language|Khoikhoi]] "dachab". The word "dagga" has been extended to include the genus ''[[Cannabis]]'' in Afrikaans and [[South African English]], so the use of "wild" serves to distinguish ''Leonotis'' from ''Cannabis''.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.etymonline.com/index.php?term=dagga |title=Online Etymology Dictionary |website=Etymonline.com |access-date=8 February 2016}}</ref>
[[Image:Leonotis leonurus flower.jpg|thumb]]

==Description==
The shrub grows {{convert|2|to|3|m|ft|0}} tall (rarely to {{cvt|4|m}}), and {{cvt|1.5|m|ft|0}} wide, with softly woody stems.<ref name="sanbi"/><ref name="SchmidtLotter2002">{{cite book |author1=Ernst Schmidt |author2=Mervyn Lotter |author3=Warren McCleland |title=Trees and Shrubs of Mpumalanga and Kruger National Park |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RpVJJH3kV0oC&pg=PA586 |year=2002 |publisher=Jacana Media |isbn=978-1-919777-30-6 |pages=586–}}</ref> The leaves are medium-dark green, {{convert|5|-|10|cm|0}} long, and aromatic when crushed. The plant has hairy tubular 4–5 cm orange flowers, 3–11 together in tiered whorls ([[verticillaster]]s) typical of the mint family, that encircle the square stems.<ref name="sanbi"/><ref name="SchmidtLotter2002"/> They rise up to {{cvt|0.9|m}} above the foliage, with flowering in summer (November to January) in some areas, but autumn to winter (April to June) in other areas.<ref name="sanbi"/>

===Variation in flower colour===
A white-flowered variety ''Leonotis leonurus'' var. ''albiflora'' was described by [[George Bentham]],<ref name="sanbi"/> but is not now accepted as distinct at [[variety (botany)|varietal rank]];<ref name="POWO"/> yellow cultivars also exist.

===Ecology===
The native [[habitat]] of ''Leonotis leonurus'' is among rocks and in grasslands of southern Africa, particularly in wetter eastern and southern areas.<ref name="sanbi"/><ref name="Quattrocchi2016">{{cite book |author=Umberto Quattrocchi |title=CRC World Dictionary of Medicinal and Poisonous Plants: Common Names, Scientific Names, Eponyms, Synonyms, and Etymology (5 Volume Set) |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-37OBQAAQBAJ&pg=PA2244 |date=19 April 2016 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=978-1-4822-5064-0 |pages=2244–}}</ref> It attracts nectivorous birds (mainly [[sunbird]]s), as well as various insects such as bees and butterflies.<ref name="sanbi"/> The flowers' mainly orange to orange-red colour and tubular shape are indicative of its co-evolution with African sunbirds, which have curved bills suited to feeding from tubular flowers. The butterfly ''[[Cacyreus lingeus]]'' (Lycenidae) uses the foliage as a larval food plant.<ref name="sanbi"/>

==Cultivation==
''Leonotis leonurus'' is cultivated as an [[ornamental plant]] for its copious orange blossom spikes, and is used as specimen shrub or a screen in gardens and parks.<ref name="sanbi"/> It is moderately [[xeriscaping|drought tolerant]], and a nectar source for birds and butterflies in landscape settings.<ref name="sanbi"/> It was introduced to Europe in the 1600s.<ref name="SchmidtLotter2002"/>

Lion's ear can be found introduced as an [[ornamental plant]] in other subtropical and [[Mediterranean climate]] regions beyond South Africa, such as California, Hawaii,<ref name="usda">{{cite web |url=https://plants.usda.gov/java/profile?symbol=LELE3 |title=PLANTS Profile for ''Leonotis leonurus'' (lion's ear) |author= |date= |website= |publisher=[[United States Department of Agriculture]] [[Natural Resources Conservation Service]] |access-date=28 March 2010}}</ref> and Australia where it has [[naturalisation (biology)|naturalised]] in some areas. In cooler climates it is used as an [[annual plant|annual]] and winter [[Conservatory (greenhouse)|conservatory]] plant.<ref name="mbc">[http://www.mobot.org/gardeninghelp/plantfinder/Plant.asp?code=A525 MBC-Kemper Center - ''Leonotis leonurus'']{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} . accessed 7.7.2011</ref>

==Pharmacology and toxicology==
Marrubiin has both antioxidant and cardioprotective properties and has shown to significantly improve myocardial function.<ref>Popoola KO Elbagory AM, Ameer F, Hussein AA. Marrubiin. Molecules 2013; 18(18):9049-9060.</ref><ref>XinHua, 2010</ref>

[[Docosatetraenoylethanolamide]] (DEA) is a cannabinoid that acts on the [[Cannabinoid receptor type 1|cannabinoid (CB<sub>1</sub>) receptor]] which has been found in the whole flower extract of the putative variety ''Leonotis leonurus'' var. ''albiflora''.<ref>{{cite journal |url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/346796873 |title=Toward the identification of a phytocannabinoid-like compound in the flowers of a South African medicinal plant (''Leonotis leonurus'') |date=December 2020 |journal=BMC Research Notes |volume=13 |issue=1 |doi=10.1186/s13104-020-05372-z |author1=Ethan Hunter |author2=Marietjie Aletta Stander |author3=Jens Kossmann |author4=S. Chakraborty |page=522 |pmid=33172494 |pmc=7653773 |access-date=17 May 2022 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

''Leonotis leonurus'' contains several labdane diterpene–based compounds such as Hispanolone, Leonurun, Leonurine and Leoleorins. C-N<ref name="phytojournal.com"/>

[[Leonurine]] (also known as SCM-198 in research) is a pseudoalkaloid that has been isolated from Leonotis leonurus, Leonotis nepetifolia, Leonurus japonicus, Leonurus cardiaca (motherwort), Leonurus sibiricus, as well as other plants of family Lamiaceae.{{Citation needed|date=September 2025}} Leonurine is easily extracted into water.<ref name=NewStar>{{cite web|url=http://www.newstar-chem.com/english/display.asp?id=208|title=The Leonurine and its preparation|date=2008|publisher=An Hui New Star Pharmaceutical Development Co.|access-date=2008-08-28|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080515223641/http://www.newstar-chem.com/english/display.asp?id=208|archive-date=2008-05-15}}</ref>
One experimental animal study suggests that the aqueous leaf extract of ''Leonotis leonurus'' possesses [[nociception|antinociceptive]], [[inflammation|antiinflammatory]], and [[hypoglycemic]] properties.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Ojewole JA |title=Antinociceptive, antiinflammatory and antidiabetic effects of ''Leonotis leonurus'' (L.) R. BR. [Lamiaceae] leaf aqueous extract in mice and rats |journal=Methods and Findings in Experimental and Clinical Pharmacology |volume=27 |issue=4 |pages=257–64 |date=May 2005 |pmid=16082426 |doi=10.1358/mf.2005.27.4.893583}}</ref>

An animal study in rats indicated that in high doses, lion's ear has significant toxicological adverse effects on organs, red blood cells, white blood cells, and other important bodily functions. Acute toxicity tests in animals caused death for those receiving a 3200 mg/kg dose. A 1600 mg/kg dose of whole plant extract led to changes in red blood cells, haemoglobin concentration, mean corpuscular volume, platelets, and white blood cells.<ref>{{cite journal |pmid=19244291 |year=2008 |last1=Maphosa |first1=V |last2=Masika |first2=P |last3=Adedapo |first3=A |title=Safety evaluation of the aqueous extract of ''Leonotis leonurus'' shoots in rats |volume=27 |issue=11 |pages=837–43 |doi=10.1177/0960327108099533 |journal=Human & Experimental Toxicology |bibcode=2008HETox..27..837M |s2cid=27776434}}</ref>

==Traditional uses==
Infusions made from flowers, seeds, leaves, or stems are widely used to treat [[tuberculosis]], [[jaundice]], [[muscle cramps]], [[high blood pressure]], [[diabetes]], [[viral hepatitis]], [[dysentery]], and [[diarrhoea]].<ref>Van WJB, van OB, Gericke N. Medicinal plants of South Africa. Briza Publications. Cape Town, 2000.</ref><ref>Noumi E, Houngue F, Lontsi D. Traditional medicines in primary health care: plants used for the treatment of hypertension in Bafia, Cameroon. Fitoterapia 1999; 70(2):134-139.</ref> The leaves, roots, and bark are used as an [[emetic]] for snakebites, and bee and scorpion stings.<ref>Hutchings AH, Scott G, Lewis AB. Cunningham, Zulu medicinal plants, an Inventory. Natal University Press, Pietermaritzburg, 1996, 266-267.</ref> The fresh stem juice is used as an infusion drink for "[[four humors|blood impurity]]" in some parts of South Africa.<ref>Watt JM, Breyer BMG. Medicinal and poisonous plants of Southern Africa. E & S Livingstone. Edinburg, 1962.</ref>

==Legal status==
===Latvia===
''Leonotis leonurus'' has been illegal in [[Latvia]] since November 2009, and is classified as a Schedule 1 drug. Possession of quantities up to 1 gram are fined up to 280 euros. Possession and distribution of larger quantities can be punished with up to 15 years in prison.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.likumi.lv/doc.php?mode=DOC&id=50539 |title=Par Krimināllikuma spēkā stāšanās un piemērošanas kārtību |publisher=[[likumi.lv]] |date= |access-date=2013-06-23 |language=Latvian}}</ref>

===Poland===
''Leonotis leonurus'' was banned in [[Poland]] in March 2009. Possession and distribution lead to criminal charges.<ref>{{in lang|pl}} [http://isap.sejm.gov.pl/DetailsServlet?id=WDU20090630520 Dz.U. 2009 nr 63 poz. 520], Internetowy System Aktów Prawnych.</ref>
